overview: This record refers to Sukhothai, a Tai kingdom in what is now Thailand, conventionally dated from 1238 to incorporation into Ayutthaya in 1438. The imported 1100 to 1200 map interval is too early for that kingdom. Its enormous outline also extends far beyond Sukhothai’s central Thai heartland and is not a dependable historical border. The evidence below concerns the later kingdom and the continuing life of its towns, rather than a Sukhothai empire in 1100.

periods.title: The historical kingdom
periods.summary: Sukhothai developed distinctive urban, religious and artistic institutions.

periods.title: Crafts under later rulers
periods.summary: Ceramic production continued beyond the kingdom’s political independence.

items.text: Sukhothai belonged to a network of important towns. Si Satchanalai combined monasteries with a major pottery industry, while Kamphaeng Phet guarded southern approaches and trade routes. Looking at all three changes the picture from one royal capital to a connected landscape of worship, work, transport and defense.

Dams, reservoirs, ponds and canals helped manage seasonal water. Their purposes included agriculture, ordinary water supply, communication and ritual, while moats also protected urban spaces. Keeping a town working required more than building temples: people had to guide water to useful places and cope with flooding. Surviving earthworks reveal that practical engineering beneath the famous monuments.

Excavations at Ban Ko Noi and Ban Pa Yang, beside the Yom River near Si Satchanalai, revealed successive types of pottery kilns. The Thai Ceramic Archaeology Project investigated them intensively during the 1980s. Comparing underground and later surface kilns showed that workshop technology changed over time. Researchers still use approximate and sometimes differing dates for the earliest production phases.

A small stoneware tube in the Asian Civilisations Museum was a useful workshop tool. Supports of this kind helped potters fire vessels of different sizes with less risk of pieces sticking together. Circular marks on vessel bases can record where the supports touched them. A mark that looks like a blemish can therefore explain how a whole kiln load was stacked.

Not every firing worked. A fifteenth-century Sukhothai bowl fragment in the British Museum is still attached to its circular kiln support. Its fish decoration survives, but the bowl failed to separate cleanly from its equipment. This workshop reject preserves a small manufacturing mishap. The museum records it as a field-collected fragment, rather than a precisely excavated household object.

Pottery recovered from the Ko Khram shipwreck helped overturn an older story that Sukhothai’s kilns had finished working before Si Satchanalai’s industry developed. Both centers operated during part of the same period, including the fifteenth century. Sukhothai ceramics also reached places in Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan. Their journeys continued across changes of political ruler.

The Ram Khamhaeng inscription describes inheritance through a household’s land, rice stores, animals and dependents. Its list includes wives and children within a father’s estate. That wording reveals a hierarchical family world, quite different from modern equal individual rights. This is a royal text’s description of order, not a survey proving that every family lived alike.

The same inscription describes a Kathina festival with gifts to monks, flowers, cushions and pillows, followed by a procession with music and singing. It presents religious giving as a social occasion as well as a sacred duty. Because the text praises its ruler and its dating is debated, this lively account should be read as its portrayal of the city.

Artists made the Buddha appear in motion as well as seated in meditation. A bronze Walking Buddha now in Saint Louis dates to the fourteenth or fifteenth century and stands about 38 centimeters high. Such a surviving object brings the artistic tradition down from monumental scale to something a child can measure with a ruler. Its museum date spans the kingdom’s later history.

At Wat Si Chum, slate panels combine carved pictures with short Thai captions about the Buddha’s previous lives. Panel 27 shows a teaching ascetic, a king and another ascetic lying down; its story compares a renouncer’s happiness with a king’s. These were illustrated lessons in a temple passage. Scholars debate their precise dates, placing them within the late medieval Sukhothai tradition.

sections.title: A surviving voice and its discovery

items.text: “ในน้ำมีปลา” means “there is fish in the water”. This is a modern Thai transcription of words on face 1, lines 18 to 19, of the Ram Khamhaeng inscription, traditionally dated 1292. The original letter shapes differ. Its authorship and date have been debated, so the famous phrase is a sample from a specific surviving text, not independent proof that everyone had enough food.

Prince Mongkut, then a Buddhist monk and later King Rama IV, found the inscription at old Sukhothai in 1833, according to the National Archives’ account. Writing covers four faces of the stone, now held in Bangkok’s National Museum. Its rediscovery made an old royal account available to later readers, who have continued to argue about how best to interpret it.

ending.text: Sukhothai was incorporated into Ayutthaya in 1438. That political ending did not erase its communities or artistic traditions. Pottery production and exchange continued under later rulers. The imported map endpoint of 1200 is therefore neither the kingdom’s actual end nor an abandonment date for its towns.
